description: Greedy Algorithms track: 4 lessons, 10 knowledge checks, 7 practice problems.

coding.title: Assign Cookies
coding.problemStatement:
Each child i has a greed factor `g[i]`: the smallest cookie size that will make them content. Each cookie j has size `s[j]`. Every child gets at most one cookie, and every cookie goes to at most one child.

Maximise the number of content children.
coding.inputFormat: Line 1: n. Line 2: the n greed factors. Line 3: m. Line 4: the m cookie sizes.
coding.outputFormat: The maximum number of content children.

examples.explanation: Both cookies have size 1, which only satisfies the first child.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
input()
g = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
input()
s = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
child = 0
for cookie in s:                    # smallest cookies first
    if child < len(g) and cookie >= g[child]:
        child += 1                  # the least greedy child left takes the smallest cookie that works
print(child)

coding.title: Lemonade Change
coding.problemStatement:
Lemonade costs $5. Customers queue up and each pays with a single $5, $10 or $20 bill. You start with no money and must give every customer the correct change from the bills you've collected so far.

Print `YES` if you can give everyone correct change, otherwise `NO`.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains the n bills in queue order.

examples.explanation: After the two $10s you hold two $10 bills and no $5 — you can't make $15 change.

coding.title: Maximum Non-Overlapping Meetings
coding.problemStatement:
Each meeting runs from its start time up to, but not including, its end time. You can attend at most one meeting at a time, but one may start exactly when another ends.

What is the largest number of meetings you can attend?
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. Each of the next n lines contains a meeting's start and end.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
import sys

n = int(input())
meetings = [tuple(map(int, sys.stdin.readline().split())) for _ in range(n)]
meetings.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])     # earliest end first
count, free_at = 0, -1
for start, end in meetings:
    if start >= free_at:              # fits after the last one we took
        count += 1
        free_at = end
print(count)

coding.title: Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons
coding.problemStatement:
Balloons are stretched horizontally along a line; balloon i covers the **closed** interval `[start, end]`. An arrow shot straight up at position x bursts every balloon with `start <= x <= end`.

Find the minimum number of arrows that burst all the balloons.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. Each of the next n lines contains a balloon's start and end.

examples.explanation: An arrow at 6 bursts [2, 8] and [1, 6]; one at 11 bursts [10, 16] and [7, 12].
Touching ends share a point: arrows at 2 and 4.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
import sys

n = int(input())
balloons = [tuple(map(int, sys.stdin.readline().split())) for _ in range(n)]
balloons.sort(key=lambda b: b[1])     # earliest end first
arrows, last = 0, None
for start, end in balloons:
    if last is None or start > last:  # the last arrow misses this balloon
        arrows += 1
        last = end                    # shoot as far right as possible while still hitting it
print(arrows)

coding.title: Jump Game
coding.problemStatement: You start at index 0 of an array. `a[i]` is the **maximum** number of steps you may jump forward from index i (you can also jump fewer). Can you reach the last index?
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. The second line contains the n jump lengths.

examples.explanation: Every route lands on index 3, whose 0 is a dead end.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
input()
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
farthest = 0
for i, jump in enumerate(a):
    if i > farthest:
        break                     # index i can't be reached
    farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
print("YES" if farthest >= len(a) - 1 else "NO")

coding.title: Gas Station
coding.problemStatement:
n gas stations stand on a circular road. Station i has `gas[i]` units of fuel, and driving from station i to station i + 1 (the last one leads back to station 0) uses `cost[i]` units. Your tank is unlimited but starts empty.

Find the index of the station where you can start and drive all the way round, back to it. Print `-1` if no start works. When a solution exists, it is unique.
coding.inputFormat: Line 1: n. Line 2: gas[0] … gas[n − 1]. Line 3: cost[0] … cost[n − 1].

examples.explanation: Starting at 3: tank 4−1 = 3, then 3+5−2 = 6, 6+1−3 = 4, 4+2−4 = 2, 2+3−5 = 0. Never negative.
There is less gas in total (9) than the trip costs (10).

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
input()
gas = list(map(int, input().split()))
cost = list(map(int, input().split()))
if sum(gas) < sum(cost):
    print(-1)                       # not enough fuel in total: no start can work
else:
    start, tank = 0, 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:                # can't get past i from `start`, nor from anything in between
            start, tank = i + 1, 0
    print(start)

coding.title: Job Sequencing for Maximum Profit
coding.problemStatement:
Each job takes exactly one unit of time and has a deadline d and a profit p: you earn p only if the job is **finished by time d** (that is, it runs in one of the time slots 1, 2, …, d). You can run one job per time slot.

Choose which jobs to run to maximise the total profit.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n. Each of the next n lines contains a job's deadline and profit.

examples.explanation: Run the 27 job in slot 1, the 100 job in slot 2 and the 15 job in slot 3.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
import sys

n = int(input())
jobs = [tuple(map(int, sys.stdin.readline().split())) for _ in range(n)]
jobs.sort(key=lambda j: -j[1])        # most profitable first
max_d = max(d for d, _ in jobs)
parent = list(range(max_d + 1))       # parent chain leads to the latest free slot <= t (0 = none)

def free_slot(t):
    while parent[t] != t:
        parent[t] = parent[parent[t]]
        t = parent[t]
    return t

total = 0
for d, p in jobs:
    slot = free_slot(d)               # as late as possible, leaving early slots for tighter deadlines
    if slot > 0:
        total += p
        parent[slot] = slot - 1       # slot is now used
print(total)

mcqs.title: Greedy check: when greedy goes wrong
mcqs.explanation: Taking the largest coin first pays 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 — three coins. The best answer is 3 + 3, two coins. Greedy is only correct when you can prove the local choice is safe; for arbitrary coin systems you need dynamic programming.
mcqs.codeSnippet:
coins = [4, 3, 1]
amount, used = 6, 0
for c in coins:          # largest coin first
    while amount >= c:
        amount -= c
        used += 1
print(used)

mcqs.title: Greedy check: which cookie to give
mcqs.questionText: Assigning cookies, you consider the least greedy child first. Which cookie should they get?
mcqs.explanation: Giving a bigger cookie than necessary can only take it away from a greedier child who needs it. Exchange argument: any optimal assignment can be rearranged to give the smallest sufficient cookie here without losing anyone.

options.optionText: The smallest cookie that satisfies them
The largest cookie available
Any cookie that satisfies them
The smallest cookie overall, even if too small

mcqs.title: Greedy check: keeping the useful bills
mcqs.questionText: A customer pays $20, and you hold both $10 and $5 bills. Why give $10 + $5 rather than three $5s?
mcqs.explanation: Both options make $15. Spending a $10 keeps more $5s, and any future situation you can handle with the other choice you can also handle with this one. That's what makes the greedy choice safe.

options.optionText: $5 bills are needed for every kind of change, while $10s only help with $20s — so keep the $5s
It uses fewer bills, which is required
Three $5s is not valid change
It makes no difference

mcqs.title: Greedy check: which order for activity selection
mcqs.questionText: To attend as many non-overlapping meetings as possible, you sort the meetings and repeatedly take the next one that fits. By what should you sort?
mcqs.explanation: The meeting that ends first leaves the most time for everything else; swapping it into any optimal schedule never makes it worse. Earliest start can pick one long meeting that blocks many; shortest first fails on a short meeting that overlaps two long, compatible ones.

options.optionText: Earliest end time first
Earliest start time first
Shortest duration first
Latest start time first

mcqs.title: Greedy check: where to shoot
mcqs.questionText: With balloons sorted by end, the first balloon not yet burst has interval [s, e]. Where should the next arrow go?
mcqs.explanation: This balloon must be hit, and among points that hit it, e also hits every balloon that starts before e — the most of anything you could pick. Any balloon starting after e needs a new arrow.

options.optionText: At e — as far right as possible while still hitting this balloon
At s
At the midpoint of [s, e]
At the start of the next balloon

mcqs.title: Greedy check: counting arrows
mcqs.explanation: Sorted by end: [1, 6], [2, 8], [7, 12], [10, 16]. Arrow at 6 bursts the first two; [7, 12] starts after 6, so a new arrow at 12 bursts it and [10, 16].
mcqs.codeSnippet:
balloons = [(10, 16), (2, 8), (1, 6), (7, 12)]
balloons.sort(key=lambda b: b[1])
arrows, last = 0, None
for s, e in balloons:
    if last is None or s > last:
        arrows += 1
        last = e
print(arrows)

mcqs.title: Greedy check: tracking the reach
mcqs.questionText: For the jump game, you scan left to right keeping `farthest`, the furthest index reachable so far. When do you know the answer is NO?
mcqs.explanation: A 0 is only a problem if you can't jump over it. Every index up to `farthest` is reachable, and each one can only extend the reach. If i > farthest, no index before i reaches i, so nothing after it is reachable either.

options.optionText: When you reach an index i greater than farthest — nothing before i can get you there
When you see a 0
When farthest stops increasing
Only after checking every possible path

mcqs.title: Greedy check: restarting the gas station scan
mcqs.questionText: Scanning from `start`, the tank first goes negative at station i. Why can you skip every start between `start` and i?
mcqs.explanation: From `start`, the tank was non-negative on arrival at every station before i. Starting later just throws away that non-negative surplus, so the tank at i can only be lower. Restarting at i + 1 makes the whole search O(n).

options.optionText: Each of them arrives at i with no more fuel than starting at `start` did, so they fail at i too
Those stations have no gas
Because the answer is always after i
You can't — they must each be tried

mcqs.title: Greedy check: proving a greedy choice
mcqs.explanation: Take an optimal solution that disagrees with greedy at the first step, swap in the greedy choice, and show the result is still valid and no worse. Repeat — greedy's answer is optimal. If no such swap works, greedy is probably wrong for that problem.

options.optionText: That any optimal solution can be changed step by step to include the greedy choice without getting worse
That greedy is faster than dynamic programming
That the greedy answer is unique
That every choice is equally good

mcqs.title: Greedy check: where to place a job
mcqs.questionText: In job sequencing, the most profitable remaining job has deadline d. Which time slot should it take?
mcqs.explanation: Using the latest possible slot keeps earlier slots free for jobs with tighter deadlines. Taking slot 1 for a job due at time 5 could block a job due at time 1. Union-find finds "the latest free slot <= d" in nearly O(1).

options.optionText: The latest free slot at or before d
The earliest free slot
Slot d, or skip the job if slot d is taken
Any free slot

lessons.title: Greedy algorithms: take the best choice now
lessons.summary: A greedy algorithm commits to the locally best option at each step — fast and simple, but only correct when you can prove the choice is safe.
objectives: Describe what makes an algorithm greedy
Recognise a counterexample where greedy fails
Justify a greedy rule by arguing it never makes things worse
lessons.concept:
A **greedy algorithm** builds a solution one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best **right now**, and never reconsidering. When it works, it's usually a sort plus a single pass — O(n log n) or better.

The catch: looking best now doesn't always mean best overall. Paying 6 with coins {4, 3, 1}, "largest coin first" takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 uses two. So every greedy rule needs a reason it's **safe**:

> Some optimal solution makes the same first choice as greedy.

Then greedy's first choice loses nothing, and the same argument applies to what remains.

## Two quick examples

**Cookies.** Sort children by greed and cookies by size. Give each child, least greedy first, the **smallest** cookie that satisfies them. A bigger cookie would be wasted on them and might be exactly what a greedier child needs.

**Change.** For a $20, give $10 + $5 if you can, otherwise three $5s. A $5 is useful for any change, a $10 only for $20s, so keeping $5s never hurts.
lessons.example:
Cookies: greed `[1, 2, 3]`, sizes `[1, 1]` → sorted, then two pointers:

| cookie | child waiting (greed) | satisfied? | content children |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | yes | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | no — cookie skipped | 1 |

```python
g.sort(); s.sort()
child = 0
for cookie in s:
    if child < len(g) and cookie >= g[child]:
        child += 1
print(child)
```

Lemonade `[5, 5, 10, 10, 20]`: after the two $10s you hold two $10 bills and no $5. The $20 needs $15 — impossible, so the answer is NO. No other choice earlier could have helped: each $10 needed a $5 back.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Trusting a greedy rule without a reason.** Try small counterexamples first (like the coins above).
- **Forgetting to sort.** Most greedy algorithms only work in a specific order.
- **Giving more than necessary** (the largest cookie, three $5s when a $10 would do) — it wastes resources a later step needs.
- **Assuming greedy is always optimal for coin change.** It is for some coin systems (like 1, 5, 10, 25), not in general.

lessons.title: Interval scheduling: sort by end
lessons.summary: To fit the most intervals, or stab them with the fewest points, sort by end time and sweep once.
objectives: Select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals
Find the minimum number of points that stab every interval
Explain why sorting by end — not start or length — is correct
lessons.concept:
## Activity selection

To attend as many meetings as possible, sort them by **end time** and take each meeting that starts at or after the end of the last one you took.

```python
meetings.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])
count, free_at = 0, -inf
for start, end in meetings:
    if start >= free_at:
        count += 1
        free_at = end
```

**Why the earliest end?** Take any optimal schedule and look at its first meeting. Swapping it for the meeting that ends earliest overall keeps every later meeting compatible — it ends no later. Repeat: greedy's choices are always as good. Other rules fail: earliest *start* can pick one long meeting that blocks many; *shortest* first can pick a short meeting that overlaps two compatible long ones.

## Stabbing intervals (balloons)

Each arrow at x bursts every balloon covering x. Sort by end. The first balloon must be hit somehow, and shooting at its **end** hits it plus everything that starts by then — nothing to its right would do better. Skip the balloons it bursts; the next balloon starting after that point needs a new arrow.

The two problems are linked: the minimum number of arrows equals the maximum number of balloons that are pairwise disjoint.

Watch the boundaries: half-open meetings `[s, e)` may touch (`start >= free_at`); closed balloons `[s, e]` that touch share a point (`start > last` needs a new arrow).

**What it costs.** Sorting dominates: O(n log n). The scan afterwards is a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra memory, in both problems.
lessons.example:
Meetings `(1,3) (2,4) (3,5) (0,7) (5,9) (8,10)` sorted by end:

| meeting | starts after last end? | take? | free at |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1, 3) | yes | ✓ | 3 |
| (2, 4) | 2 < 3 | | 3 |
| (3, 5) | 3 >= 3 | ✓ | 5 |
| (0, 7) | 0 < 5 | | 5 |
| (5, 9) | 5 >= 5 | ✓ | 9 |
| (8, 10) | 8 < 9 | | 9 |

Three meetings.

```cpp
sort(b.begin(), b.end());                 // pairs (end, start)
int arrows = 0; long long last; bool any = false;
for (auto& [e, s] : b)
    if (!any || s > last) { arrows++; last = e; any = true; }
```
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Sorting by start time.** It's the natural first guess and it's wrong for maximising the count.
- **Getting touching endpoints wrong.** Read whether intervals are closed or half-open.
- **Initialising the "last end" to 0** when times can be 0 or negative — use −∞ or a flag.
- **Shooting at the start of a balloon** instead of its end.

lessons.title: Greedy scans: reach and fuel
lessons.summary: Some greedy algorithms need no sorting — just one pass that tracks the best you can do so far.
objectives: Decide reachability in the jump game with a single running maximum
Find the gas station start in O(n) and justify skipping starts
Use a global check (total fuel) to decide feasibility up front
lessons.concept:
## Jump game

Every index up to some `farthest` is reachable. Scanning left to right, each reachable index i can push it to `i + a[i]`. If you ever arrive at an i beyond `farthest`, nothing before it reaches it — the end is unreachable.

```python
farthest = 0
for i, jump in enumerate(a):
    if i > farthest:
        break
    farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
reachable = farthest >= len(a) - 1
```

You never need to decide *which* jump to take — tracking the reach covers every choice at once. O(n).

## Gas station

First, a global fact: if the total gas is less than the total cost, no start works. Otherwise, scan from `start = 0` with a running tank. If the tank goes negative at station i, then **no start between `start` and i works either**: each of them would reach i with no more fuel than we had. So jump straight to `start = i + 1` with an empty tank. One pass: O(n).

When the total is non-negative, the last `start` found is the answer — the stretch after it has enough surplus to cover the deficit before it.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Treating every 0 as a dead end** in the jump game. It only matters if nothing jumps over it.
- **Trying every start for the gas station** — O(n²). Use the restart argument.
- **Forgetting the total check.** The scan alone returns *some* index even when no start works.
- **Simulating every possible jump path** — exponential. Track the reach instead.

lessons.title: Exchange arguments: job sequencing
lessons.summary: Take the most valuable items first, and place each one where it blocks the least — then prove it by swapping.
objectives: Use an exchange argument to justify a greedy algorithm
Schedule unit-time jobs with deadlines for maximum profit
Find the latest free slot quickly with union-find
lessons.concept:
An **exchange argument** is the standard proof that a greedy algorithm is optimal: take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one, **swap** in the greedy choice, and show the result is still valid and no worse. Repeating the swap turns the optimal solution into greedy's.

## Job sequencing

Each job takes one time slot and pays its profit only if it runs by its deadline. Greedy:

1. Consider jobs from the **most profitable** down.
2. Put each one in the **latest free slot** at or before its deadline; if there is none, skip it.

Why most profitable first: if an optimal schedule leaves out the top job, it can replace some other job in a slot the top job could use and earn at least as much. Why the latest slot: an earlier slot is more valuable to jobs with tighter deadlines, so using the latest one keeps the most options open.

## Finding the latest free slot fast

Scanning down from d for a free slot is O(d) per job. Instead keep a union-find where each slot points to the latest free slot at or before it (0 means none). When slot t is used, link it to t − 1. With path compression, each lookup is nearly O(1), so the algorithm is O(n log n) for the sort.

An alternative greedy works too: sort by deadline and keep a min-heap of chosen profits; whenever there are more jobs than slots up to the current deadline, drop the least profitable.
lessons.example:
Jobs (deadline, profit): `(2, 100) (1, 19) (2, 27) (1, 25) (3, 15)`, most profitable first:

| job | latest free slot <= deadline | placed? | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| (2, 100) | 2 | slot 2 | 100 |
| (2, 27) | 1 | slot 1 | 127 |
| (1, 25) | none | skip | 127 |
| (1, 19) | none | skip | 127 |
| (3, 15) | 3 | slot 3 | **142** |

```cpp
sort(jobs.rbegin(), jobs.rend());             // (profit, deadline), most profitable first
iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);        // slot t initially points to itself
for (auto& [p, d] : jobs) {
    int slot = freeSlot(d);                   // latest free slot <= d
    if (slot > 0) { total += p; parent[slot] = slot - 1; }
}
```
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Placing jobs in the earliest free slot.** It can block a job with a tighter deadline.
- **Sorting by deadline and taking jobs in that order without dropping** — you need the heap step to swap out low-profit jobs.
- **Scanning slots linearly** for every job — O(n × d). Use union-find.
- **Overflow.** 2000 jobs × 10⁶ profit exceeds 32 bits.
